scenes.visual: Carbon-count capsules: 5C + CO2 -> 6C intermediate -> two 3C PGA.
scenes.narration: Here is the first committed step drawn as simple beads on a string. Ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate is a five-carbon backbone capped at each end by a phosphate. The enzyme Rubisco grabs a single molecule of carbon dioxide and attaches it to that five-carbon chain, briefly making a six-carbon intermediate. That intermediate is unstable and immediately splits down the middle. The result is two identical three-carbon molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate. Notice the bookkeeping, one five-carbon sugar plus one carbon dioxide yields six carbons total, which divide cleanly into two threes. Counting carbons this way is the key to following the entire cycle without getting lost.

scenes.visual: Energy ledger built by phase: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO2, 9+6 per G3P, 18+12 per glucose.
scenes.narration: Let us total the energy bill as a pyramid built from the bottom up. At the base, one carbon dioxide enters. Three turns of the cycle, fixing three carbon dioxides, cost nine ATP and six NADPH, and yield one net molecule of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate. To assemble a full six-carbon glucose, you must run the cycle six times, doubling everything. Eighteen ATP and twelve NADPH per glucose. Breaking it down by phase, fixation by Rubisco is energetically free. The reduction step that turns acid into sugar costs the ATP and NADPH, and regenerating ribulose bisphosphate costs additional ATP. Sugar is expensive, and this ledger shows exactly where every high-energy molecule is spent.

scenes.visual: Domino chain: heat, stomata close, CO2 drops, O2 wins, oxygenase fires, carbon lost.
scenes.narration: Follow the dominoes that fall when a plant gets too hot. Temperature rises, so the plant closes its stomata to conserve water. But closed stomata trap the leaf. Fresh carbon dioxide can no longer enter, and internal carbon dioxide drops while oxygen builds up. Now oxygen starts winning the competition for Rubisco's active site and the enzyme misfires as an oxygenase. That wasteful oxygenase reaction burns carbon and energy for no sugar gained. Each step forces the next and the chain ends in lost productivity. This single cascade explains why hot, dry climates are so hard on ordinary plants, and it sets up the two evolutionary fixes, spatial and temporal.

scenes.visual: Carbon ledger: normal cycle gains 6 C, photorespiration loses 3 C.
scenes.narration: Compare two runs of the cycle side by side, counting carbons the whole way. On top, the normal cycle, six carbon dioxides feed in, Rubisco makes twelve molecules of 3-PGA, which become twelve G3P, ten G3P regenerate the starting sugars, two exit, and you net one glucose, a gain of six fixed carbons. On the bottom, photorespiration, Rubisco grabs oxygen instead, producing 3-PGA plus phosphoglycolate. The salvage pathway recovers some carbon but releases carbon dioxide, and you actually lose three fixed carbons. There are not even enough carbons left to regenerate the starting sugar, and no glucose is made. The contrast makes the cost unmistakable.
